fuentes/iberica-de-apiano/resumen.texto: Book VI of Appian of Alexandria’s Roman History, the only continuous ancient account of the Roman conquest of the peninsula, from the Carthaginians to Augustus. It narrates in detail the war of Segeda, the treachery of Lucullus at Cauca and that of Galba against the Lusitanians, the war of Viriathus, the Numantine war with Scipio’s siege and the campaigns of Titus Didius. It gives figures for armies and dead, names of Hispanic chiefs (Caro, Ambón, Leucón, Retógenes, Avaro, Púnico, Césaro, Tautalus) and scenes such as hunger and cannibalism at Numantia.

fuentes/iberica-de-apiano/por_que_import.texto: Almost everything told about the Celtiberian and Lusitanian wars comes from here. Appian wrote almost three centuries after the events, drawing on Polybius (a witness of the siege of Numantia), Posidonius and Roman annalists he does not name; he is more critical of treacherous Roman generals than many Latin authors, but his round figures and some speeches are literary reconstructions.

fuentes/iberica-de-apiano/leer.0.titulo.texto: English translation by Horace White (1899) at Livius.org

fuentes/iberica-de-apiano/leer.1.titulo.texto: English translation by Horace White (1899) at Perseus, by chapter

fuentes/punica-silio-italico/resumen.texto: Epic poem in seventeen books on the Second Punic War. In Book III it lists the Hispanic peoples who follow Hannibal: the Celts who “mingled their name with the Iberians”, Cantabrians, Vascones, Gallaeci, Lusitanians and others, and tells how the Celtiberians leave the bodies of those fallen in battle for the vultures, which carry them to heaven. It includes an anachronistic Viriathus among Hannibal’s Hispanic chiefs.

fuentes/punica-silio-italico/por_que_imp.texto: It is a literary source, with anachronisms, but it agrees with Aelian and with the stelae of Numantia and Tiermes on the rite of exposing the war dead to vultures. It shows how Rome viewed the Hispanic peoples in the 1st century AD.

fuentes/punica-silio-italico/leer.0.titu.texto: Latin text of Book III on Wikisource

fuentes/bronces-de-botorrita/soporte.texto: Bronze plates inscribed in Celtiberian script

fuentes/bronces-de-botorrita/resumen.texto: Four bronze plates found between 1970 and 1994 at the Cabezo de las Minas in Botorrita (Zaragoza), the ancient Contrebia Belaisca. The first (1970), inscribed on both sides, was the first long text in Celtiberian to be found (the first edition is by Javier de Hoz and Luis Michelena, 1974): one side has eleven lines that seem to regulate the use of an area or enclosure, perhaps sacred, with prohibitions and fines, and the other side a list of some fourteen names followed by the word bintis, usually understood as a magistrate’s title. The fourth (1994) is a minor fragment; the second is in Latin and the third is a long list of names (see their entries).

fuentes/bronces-de-botorrita/por_que_imp.texto: They show that the Celtiberians wrote their language, using a semi-syllabary taken from the Iberians, and that their cities had magistrates and written rules. The translation is largely uncertain: the structure and many words are understood, but not the exact meaning, and interpretations vary between religious and legal.

fuentes/botorrita-iii/resumen.texto: Large bronze plate found in 1992, the longest known Celtiberian text: after a brief heading it lists some two hundred and fifty people, each with his name, that of his kin group and that of his father, among them at least twenty-seven women. The purpose of the list is debated: a census, the members of an agreement or the beneficiaries of a distribution.

fuentes/botorrita-iii/por_que_importa.texto: It is the largest collection of Celtiberian names from a single place and allows the study of onomastics and of organization into kin groups, which appear in the plural genitive. It is the basis of what is known about Celtiberian “gentilitates”.

fuentes/tabula-contrebiensis/resumen.texto: Judgment in Latin, dated May 87 BC, in a lawsuit between the Salluienses (of Salduie, the future Caesaraugusta) and the Allavonenses over the purchase from the Sosinestani of land to build a canal. The governor Gaius Valerius Flaccus entrusted the trial to the senate of Contrebia with a formula of Roman law, and the Contrebian judges ruled in favour of the Salluienses. The plate was found in 1979.

fuentes/tabula-contrebiensis/por_que_imp.texto: It is the oldest judicial document from Roman Hispania and shows a Celtiberian city applying Roman law among native communities, seven years before the Sertorian War began. It also shows the value of irrigation water in the Ebro valley.

fuentes/teseras-de-hospitalidad/resumen.texto: Small bronze plates in the shape of animals (pig, bull, dolphin, horse), of joined hands or geometric, which each party to a hospitality pact kept as proof. They carry short texts in Celtiberian, with the word kar and the name of a city or a person (for example libiaka kortika kar, of Libia), and later in Latin. Several dozen are known.

fuentes/teseras-de-hospitalidad/por_que_.texto: They document the hospitium, the institution that, according to Diodorus (V.34), made the Celtiberians vie with one another to host strangers, and that bound people and cities together with ties of mutual protection. Many appeared on the antiquities market without context, and the authenticity of some is disputed.

fuentes/bronce-de-luzaga/resumen.texto: Bronze plate with eight lines in Celtiberian (some one hundred and twenty signs), found at the end of the 19th century in Luzaga (Guadalajara) and now of unknown whereabouts. From the words that can be recognized, among them the name of the city of Arekorata and the word kar, it is interpreted as a hospitality pact between communities.

fuentes/bronce-de-luzaga/por_que_importa.texto: It was one of the first long Celtiberian texts known and it helped in deciphering the language. It uses the western variant of the script, which distinguishes voiceless and voiced consonants.

fuentes/monedas-celtibericas/soporte.texto: Silver denarii and bronze asses and fractions

fuentes/monedas-celtibericas/resumen.texto: Coins minted by Celtiberian cities from the mid-2nd century BC until the Sertorian War, with a male head on the obverse and a horseman with a spear on the reverse, and the name of the city in Celtiberian script: sekaisa (Segeda), arekorata, bilbilis, sekobirikes (Segobriga), turiasu (Turiaso), kontebakom (Contrebia), titiakos (of the Titii) and dozens more.

fuentes/monedas-celtibericas/por_que_imp.texto: They are the most abundant source in the Celtiberian language and they allow the location of cities that ancient authors only name. It is debated why they began minting: to pay troops, to pay tribute to Rome, or because of the cities’ own development.

fuentes/cabeco-das-fraguas/autor.texto: Lusitanian community of Cabeço das Fráguas

fuentes/cabeco-das-fraguas/soporte.texto: Inscription carved in rock, in Latin letters

fuentes/cabeco-das-fraguas/resumen.texto: Text carved into a rock at the summit of Cabeço das Fráguas, near Guarda (Portugal), listing animal offerings to deities: a sheep (oilam) to Trebopala, a pig (porcom) to Laebo, a bull (taurom) to Reve, among others. It recalls the Roman sacrifice of pig, sheep and bull (suovetaurilia). The proposed dates range from the 1st century BC to the 2nd century AD.

fuentes/cabeco-das-fraguas/por_que_impor.texto: It is the best-known text in Lusitanian and the centre of the debate over whether that language is Celtic: porcom preserves the Indo-European p, which Celtic lost, so Tovar, Gorrochategui, Villar and Blanca María Prósper (1999) consider it a non-Celtic Indo-European language, while Untermann (1987) and Dagmar Wodtko (2010) stress the place and personal names it shares with Celtic.

fuentes/inscripciones-lusitanas/titulo.texto: Lusitanian inscriptions of Lamas de Moledo and Arroyo de la Luz

fuentes/inscripciones-lusitanas/resumen.texto: The other long inscriptions in Lusitanian. That of Lamas de Moledo (Castro Daire, Portugal) begins in Latin, “Rufinus and Tiro wrote it”, and continues in Lusitanian with the offering of a pig (porgom) to local deities. The Arroyo de la Luz inscriptions (Cáceres) are three, the last published by Francisco Villar and Rosa Pedrero in 2001.

fuentes/inscripciones-lusitanas/por_que_.texto: Together with Cabeço das Fráguas they are almost all that survives of Lusitanian: some six inscriptions of some length. That it survives only in writing after the conquest, and in Latin letters, suggests that it was not written down before.

fuentes/bronce-de-lascuta/resumen.texto: Decree of the general Lucius Aemilius Paullus, of January 189 BC, declaring free the inhabitants of the Torre Lascutana, serfs of those of Hasta, and leaving them possession of their lands for as long as the people and the Senate of Rome wish. It was found in the 19th century at Alcalá de los Gazules (Cádiz) and is now in the Louvre.

fuentes/bronce-de-lascuta/por_que_import.texto: It is the oldest Latin document from the peninsula. It shows that Rome was already intervening in the social organization of the peoples of the south, freeing a dependent community to win its loyalty.

fuentes/bronce-de-alcantara/resumen.texto: Plaque found in 1983 at Alcántara (Cáceres) recording the unconditional surrender (deditio) of a people of Lusitania, whose name is read incomplete (Seano...), before the general Lucius Caesius in 104 BC, and the return, by the general’s decision, of their lands, buildings, laws and goods.

fuentes/bronce-de-alcantara/por_que_impo.texto: It is the only text that describes the procedure of deditio, the total surrender to Rome’s discretion that the literary sources mention in the wars in Hispania (and which was demanded of Numantia). It shows that after the surrender restitution could follow.

fuentes/edicto-del-bierzo/resumen.texto: Edict of Augustus, issued at Narbonne in 15 BC, granting immunity to the castellani Paemeiobrigenses, of the gens of the Susarri, for having remained loyal while others rebelled, and confirming their lands; in exchange, those of the castle of the Aiiobrigiaecini, of the gens of the Gigurri, must bear the burdens together with the Susarri. It names a Transduriana province that appears in no other source. It came to light in 1999 in El Bierzo (León), in confused circumstances: there are four versions of the place of discovery.

fuentes/edicto-del-bierzo/por_que_import.texto: It is direct testimony to the end of the Asturian wars and to how Rome rewarded the loyal castros. The Transduriana province and the find without context led to doubts about its authenticity: Patrick Le Roux and John Richardson were sceptical, and Alicia M. Canto listed thirty-two anomalies in lettering, metal and wording; Géza Alföldy defended it from the outset, and most specialists accept it.

fuentes/pacto-de-los-zoelas/resumen.texto: Bronze plaque recording how in 27 AD the gentilitates of the Desoncos and of the Tridiavi, both of the gens of the Zoelae, an Asturian people, renewed an ancient pact of hospitality and clientship, and how in 152 AD other people joined the agreement.

fuentes/pacto-de-los-zoelas/por_que_impo.texto: It shows that the organization of the Asturians into gentes and gentilitates was still alive a century and a half after the conquest, now written in Latin and in Roman form. It is one of the key sources on kinship and hospitality among the peoples of the north.

fuentes/el-cerco-de-numancia/resumen.texto: Tragedy in four acts on the last year of Scipio’s siege. Alongside Numantines and Romans appear allegorical figures (Spain, the river Duero, War, Hunger, Fame), and the Duero prophesies the future greatness of Spain. It follows the version of Florus and Orosius: the Numantines burn their possessions and kill themselves, and the last of them, the boy Bariatus, throws himself from a tower so that Scipio will have no one to lead in his triumph.

fuentes/el-cerco-de-numancia/por_que_imp.texto: It made Numantia the great symbol of Hispanic resistance. The work remained unpublished until 1784, and since then it has been staged in times of war, such as Rafael Alberti’s adaptation in besieged Madrid in 1937 or Jean-Louis Barrault’s in Paris that same year. Critics debate whether it exalts the imperial Spain of Philip II or, by showing Roman cruelty, criticizes the conquest.

fuentes/numantia-schulten/titulo.texto: Numantia. Results of the Excavations from 1905 to 1912

fuentes/numantia-schulten/resumen.texto: Four volumes: the Celtiberians and their wars with Rome (1914), the city of Numantia (1931), the camps of Scipio (1927) and the camps of Renieblas (1929). Schulten reconstructed the siege of 134–133 BC, with the seven camps and the circumvallation wall that Appian describes, and attributed the superimposed camps of Renieblas to Cato, Nobilior and other generals.

fuentes/numantia-schulten/por_que_import.texto: It is the basis of Roman military archaeology in Hispania, and it first documented the camps. He has been criticized for forcing the remains to fit Appian, for several of his attributions and dates having been corrected by later excavations, and for paying little attention to the native city, which the official Spanish commission was excavating in parallel.

fuentes/tartessos-schulten/titulo.texto: Tartessos. A Contribution to the Oldest History of the West

fuentes/tartessos-schulten/resumen.texto: Schulten argued that Tartessos was a great city at the mouth of the Guadalquivir, founded by Tyrrhenians from the Aegean; he searched for it without success in Doñana, and in later works he identified it with Plato’s Atlantis. The Spanish translation appeared in 1924.

fuentes/tartessos-schulten/por_que_impor.texto: It placed Tartessos at the centre of Spanish protohistory for half a century. Later historiography (for example Manuel Álvarez Martí-Aguilar, Tarteso. La construcción de un mito en la historiografía española, 2005) studies it as the construction of a myth, with forced readings of the sources and a model of eastern colonizers civilizing backward peoples. Tartessos is today understood as a culture of the lower Guadalquivir, not as a city.

fuentes/fontes-hispaniae-antiquae/resume.texto: Multi-volume collection of all the Greek and Latin texts on ancient Hispania, arranged by period, which Schulten began with Pere Bosch Gimpera in Barcelona in 1922 and which was completed in 1987 with the volume devoted to Mela, Pliny and Ptolemy.

fuentes/fontes-hispaniae-antiquae/por_qu.texto: It made it possible for the first time to work with all the ancient sources gathered together, and it was the basic tool of 20th-century Spanish ancient history. Its translations and commentaries carry Schulten’s interpretations; the series Testimonia Hispaniae Antiquae, since 1994, is replacing it.

fuentes/los-celtas-hispania-y-europa/res.texto: Volume edited by Martín Almagro-Gorbea and Gonzalo Ruiz Zapatero that brought together archaeologists and linguists on the Celts of the peninsula. It abandons Bosch Gimpera’s model of successive invasions: Almagro-Gorbea proposes a gradual Celticization over a “proto-Celtic” substratum of the Bronze Age, and Ruiz Zapatero denies that the urnfields of the northeast were Celtic.

fuentes/los-celtas-hispania-y-europa/por.texto: It marked the change of paradigm in Spain, from migrations to local processes. It is objected that it uses Celtic both for languages and for archaeological cultures, and that the “proto-Celtic” has no direct linguistic support.

fuentes/los-celtiberos-lorrio/resumen.texto: Archaeological synthesis of Celtiberia, published by the Complutense University and the University of Alicante. It follows the formation of Celtiberian culture from the 7th century BC in the upper Jalón and upper Tajo, based on necropolises, weapons, settlements and writing, and divides it into proto-Celtiberian, early, full and late phases.

fuentes/los-celtiberos-lorrio/por_que_im.texto: It is the reference work on Celtiberian archaeology. Like any synthesis based on necropolises, it depends on cemeteries excavated poorly at the beginning of the 20th century (the collections of the Marquis of Cerralbo) and on a record that over-represents warrior elites.

fuentes/los-celtiberos-burillo/titulo.texto: The Celtiberians: Ethnic Groups and States

fuentes/los-celtiberos-burillo/resumen.texto: Study that combines written sources, archaeology and numismatics to identify the Celtiberian ethnic groups (Belli, Titii, Arevaci, Lusones, Pelendones) and to argue that their great cities functioned as city-states. It places the synoecism of Segeda at the origin of the war of 153 BC. The second edition is from 2007.

fuentes/los-celtiberos-burillo/por_que_i.texto: It renewed the study of Celtiberia from the viewpoint of political history. Other authors prefer to speak of chiefdoms or of urban communities without a state, and they debate the boundaries it draws between ethnic groups, which depend on scarce sources.

fuentes/indoeuropeos-y-no-indoeuropeos/t.texto: Indo-Europeans and Non-Indo-Europeans in Pre-Roman Hispania

fuentes/indoeuropeos-y-no-indoeuropeos/r.texto: Study of the peninsula’s place names and river names in which Villar argues that, beneath the known languages, there is a layer of ancient Indo-European hydronymy that also extends across the south and east, where Iberian was spoken in historical times.

fuentes/indoeuropeos-y-no-indoeuropeos/p.texto: It is the broadest proposal for an Indo-European Hispania before the Celts. Many linguists consider that these etymologies, based on very short roots, are not enough to prove it.

fuentes/the-celts-in-the-iberian-peninsu.texto: The Celts in the Iberian Peninsula

Issue of the open-access journal e-Keltoi, of the University of Wisconsin–Milwaukee, with studies by specialists from Spain, Portugal and other countries on the Celts of the peninsula, including the synthesis by Alberto Lorrio and Gonzalo Ruiz Zapatero. It brings together different positions on the Celtiberians, the northwest, Lusitanian and religion.

It is the best open-access entry point in English into the peninsular debate, and it shows that there is no agreement on how much of what is “Celtic” in the peninsula is language, culture or a modern label.

fuentes/colectivismo-agrario-costa/resum.texto: Study by the Aragonese regenerationist on the traditions of communal ownership and communal work of the land in Spain, from the ancients to the common lands of the villages of his own time. He takes the Vaccaei of Diodorus (V.34), who divided the land and the harvest each year, as the first example of an agrarian collectivism in Hispania.

fuentes/colectivismo-agrario-costa/por_q.texto: He turned a passage of Diodorus into a precedent for the agrarian debates of the 19th and 20th centuries. He is criticized for reading a brief report, probably derived from Posidonius’s idealization of barbarians, through the eyes of the politics of his own time.

personas/istolacio/resumen.texto: Celtic chief who, with his brother, commanded troops of Iberians and Tartessians against Hamilcar Barca when he landed at Gadir (237 BC). We know him only from Diodorus (XXV.10), who says that he died in battle with his brother and that Hamilcar incorporated three thousand of the defeated into his army. He is the first Celt of the peninsula to be given a name by a source.

personas/indortes/resumen.texto: Iberian chief who gathered some fifty thousand men against Hamilcar Barca after the defeat of Istolacio. According to Diodorus (XXV.10), he fled before the battle, was captured, blinded, tortured and crucified, and Hamilcar freed ten thousand prisoners; the size of his army is the source’s figure and cannot be checked.

personas/indibil/resumen.texto: Chief of the Ilergetes, an Iberian people of the Segre valley, who first allied with Carthage and then with Scipio Africanus during the Second Punic War. He rebelled against Rome in 206 and 205 BC and died in combat. We know him from Polybius (X–XI) and Livy (XXII–XXIX).

personas/mandonio/resumen.texto: Brother of Indibilis and Ilergete chief together with him. After the defeat of the second rebellion, in 205 BC, the Ilergetes themselves handed him over to the Romans, who executed him (Livy XXIX.3).

personas/alucio/resumen.texto: Celtiberian noble whose betrothed, captured in Carthago Nova in 209 BC, was returned to him by Scipio Africanus together with the ransom gold. Livy tells it (XXVI.50) as an example of Scipio’s clemency; the episode, known as “the continence of Scipio”, was a frequent theme in European painting.

personas/olindico/resumen.texto: Celtiberian chief who around 170 BC roused his people brandishing a silver spear that, he said, had been sent to him from heaven. According to Florus (I.33.13–14), he entered the Roman camp at night to kill the consul and died beside his tent, pierced by a sentry’s pilum; Livy’s summary of Book XLIII says only that the revolt ended with his death. Florus does not mock him: he presents him as a man of great daring who, had he succeeded, would have raised all of Celtiberia. Some modern historians see in him a religious leader.

personas/punico/resumen.texto: Lusitanian chief who in 155–153 BC plundered Ulterior and, according to Appian (Iberica 56), killed some six thousand Romans. He died from a stone thrown during the siege of a city; his name, “the Punic”, is the one given by Greek and Latin sources and may be a nickname.

personas/cesaro/resumen.texto: Successor of Púnico at the head of the Lusitanians. In 153 BC, initially rejected by the praetor Lucius Mummius, he regrouped during the pursuit; according to Appian he killed some nine thousand of Mummius’s men and took his camp, arms and standards, which the Lusitanians paraded through Celtiberia (Iberica 56). Mummius, with the five thousand soldiers who remained to him, then surprised a group carrying part of the booty and recovered the standards (Iberica 57).

personas/caro-de-segeda/resumen.texto: Chief of Segeda, a city of the Belli, elected general by the Arevaci when the Segedans took refuge among them. On 23 August 153 BC, the day of the festival of Vulcan, he ambushed Nobilior’s army and killed, according to Appian (Iberica 45), six thousand Roman citizens; he died in the pursuit, attacked by the Roman cavalry that guarded the baggage.

personas/viriato/resumen.texto: Lusitanian chief who escaped the massacre of Galba (150 BC) and from 147 BC led the war against Rome for eight years according to Appian (fourteen according to the summary of Livy and Florus): he defeated Vetilius at Tribola and several praetors, and in 140 BC forced Fabius Maximus Servilianus to sign a peace that recognized him as a “friend of the Roman people”. He was killed in his sleep by three of his envoys, Audax, Ditalco and Minurus, bribed by Servilius Caepio (139 BC). We know him from Appian (Iberica 60–75), from Diodorus (XXXIII, who takes from Posidonius a moralizing portrait of the austere shepherd), from the summary of Livy, which calls him “a shepherd, then a hunter; a hunter, then a brigand, and soon a general”, and from Florus, Orosius and Cassius Dio. His precise origin is unknown. Since the Renaissance, Portugal (Camões sings of him in The Lusiads, and the Estado Novo exalted him) and Spain (the city of Zamora claims that he was born there and erected a statue to him in the early 20th century) have claimed him as a national hero, an appropriation that current historiography describes as anachronistic.

personas/tautalo/resumen.texto: Viriathus’s successor, who after a failed attack on Saguntum surrendered to Servilius Caepio in 139 BC; Caepio disarmed the Lusitanians and gave them lands (Appian, Iberica 75). He is the last chief of the war of Viriathus named by the sources.

personas/audax-ditalcon-y-minuro/resumen.texto: Three men trusted by Viriathus, from the city of Urso according to Diodorus, who went as envoys to Servilius Caepio, accepted his bribe and killed Viriathus in his sleep (139 BC). According to Appian (Iberica 74), when they came to collect, Caepio sent them on to Rome; the phrase “Rome does not pay traitors” is a modern version of what Eutropius (IV.16) and other late authors tell.

personas/retogenes/resumen.texto: Numantine noble who during Scipio’s siege crossed the Roman lines at night with five friends and five servants using a folding ladder, and toured the Arevacian cities asking for help (Appian, Iberica 94). Only the young men of Lutia wanted to go, and Scipio had their hands cut off. Appian does not tell his end. Valerius Maximus (III.2 ext. 7) tells that a Numantine named Retógenes, the noblest in the city, set fire to his quarter when all was lost and died in it; it is not certain that it was the same man.

personas/avaro-numantino/resumen.texto: Numantine who, with the city starving, went with five others to ask Scipio for terms of surrender. According to Appian (Iberica 95), when they returned with the demand for unconditional surrender, the Numantines killed him along with his companions, believing that they had negotiated their own salvation.

personas/corocota/resumen.texto: Brigand or Hispanic chief, probably Cantabrian or Asturian, for whose head Augustus offered two hundred and fifty thousand sesterces. According to Cassius Dio (LVI.43), he presented himself before the emperor, who paid him the reward and let him go free; the anecdote is the only report about him.

personas/caton-el-viejo/resumen.texto: Roman politician who, as consul in 195 BC, landed at Emporion, put down the rebellion in Citerior, and boasted of having taken more cities than the days he had spent in Hispania (Plutarch, Cato 10; Livy XXXIV.8–21). He offered the Celtiberian mercenaries who served the Turdetani double pay to switch over to Rome, and then marched against Segontia (Livy XXXIV.19). In 149 BC he prosecuted Servius Sulpicius Galba for the massacre of the Lusitanians; his Origines, the first history of Rome in Latin, survives in fragments.

personas/tiberio-sempronio-graco-mayor/r.texto: Praetor of Hispania Citerior in 180–178 BC, who ended the first Celtiberian war with treaties that fixed tribute, auxiliary troops and a prohibition on founding new cities (Appian, Iberica 43; Livy XL–XLI). He founded Gracurris (Alfaro). His peace lasted about twenty-five years, and the sources remember it as a model of fair treatment; he was the father of the tribunes Tiberius and Gaius Gracchus.

personas/quinto-fulvio-nobilior/resumen.texto: Consul in 153 BC, sent with almost thirty thousand men against Segeda. He suffered Caro’s ambush on the day of Vulcan and then failed before Numantia, where a wounded elephant scattered the others (Appian, Iberica 45–47). Because of the urgency of his campaign, the consuls began to take office on 1 January.

personas/marco-claudio-marcelo-152/nombr.texto: Marcus Claudius Marcellus (consul in 166, 155 and 152 BC)

personas/marco-claudio-marcelo-152/resum.texto: Grandson of the victor of Clastidium, consul for the third time in 152 BC, who negotiated a moderate peace with the Arevaci, Belli and Titii in 151 BC. According to Posidonius, cited by Strabo (III.4.13), he extracted six hundred talents from them. He died in a shipwreck in 148 BC.

personas/lucio-licinio-luculo-151/resume.texto: Consul who in 151 BC, without authorization from the Senate, attacked the Vaccaei. At Cauca he accepted their surrender, entered the city and killed most of its twenty thousand men; he later failed before Intercatia and Palantia (Appian, Iberica 51–55, who accuses him of seeking booty). He was not tried.

personas/servio-sulpicio-galba/resumen.texto: Praetor of Ulterior who in 150 BC promised lands to the Lusitanians, divided them into three groups, disarmed them and had them killed (Appian, Iberica 59–60). Prosecuted in Rome in 149 BC, with Cato among the accusers, he was acquitted after appearing with his children, who wept (summary of Livy XLIX; Cicero, Brutus 89–90); Appian says that he saved himself with his money. He was consul in 144 BC and one of the great orators of his time.

personas/quinto-fabio-maximo-serviliano/.texto: Consul in 142 BC and proconsul in Ulterior, who, besieged by Viriathus at Erisana (140 BC), signed a peace that recognized Viriathus as a friend of the Roman people and left him his lands; the Roman people ratified it (Appian, Iberica 69).

personas/quinto-servilio-cepion-140/resu.texto: Brother of Servilianus, he got the Senate to break the peace with Viriathus and bribed his envoys to kill him (139 BC). According to Appian (Iberica 70–75) he received the surrender of Tautalus; according to some late sources, the Senate denied him a triumph.

personas/quinto-cecilio-metelo-macedonic.texto: Conqueror of Macedonia, consul in 143 BC, who subdued the Arevaci except Termantia and Numantia. According to Valerius Maximus (V.1.5), he gave up assaulting Centobriga when its defenders put the sons of a deserter in the breach, and with that gesture he won over other Celtiberian cities.

personas/quinto-pompeyo-141/resumen.texto: Consul who failed before Numantia and Termantia and in 140 BC secretly agreed a peace with the Numantines, which he later denied before the Senate (Appian, Iberica 76–79). The Senate repudiated it and the war went on.

personas/cayo-hostilio-mancino/resumen.texto: Consul in 137 BC who, besieged by the Numantines, surrendered an army of some twenty thousand men in exchange for a treaty negotiated by his quaestor Tiberius Gracchus. The Senate rejected it and, to free Rome from the oath, handed Mancinus over naked and bound to the Numantines, who did not accept him (Appian, Iberica 80–83; Plutarch, Tiberius Gracchus 5–7).

personas/decimo-junio-bruto-galaico/resu.texto: Consul in 138 BC who led the first Roman campaign to the northwest: he crossed the Limia, which his soldiers feared as the Lethe, the river of oblivion, and then the Minho. For that campaign he received the nickname Callaicus; according to Livy, he gave lands to the former soldiers of Viriathus and founded Valentia.

personas/escipion-emiliano/resumen.texto: Roman general who destroyed Carthage in 146 BC and Numantia in 133 BC. He had served in Hispania in 151 BC, when he defeated a Vaccaean warrior in single combat at Intercatia. Elected consul in 134 BC to end the Numantine war, he surrounded the city with a siege line nine kilometres long and starved it into surrender; with him were Polybius, the poet Lucilius, Gaius Marius and the Numidian Jugurtha. He died in 129 BC in circumstances that were already suspected of being criminal in his own time.

personas/tito-didio/resumen.texto: Consul in 98 BC and proconsul of Citerior until 93 BC. According to Appian (Iberica 99–100), he killed some twenty thousand Arevaci, forced Termes down to the plain, sold the inhabitants of Colenda and lured those of a neighbouring city with the promise of land in order to massacre them. He died in the Social War.

personas/cayo-valerio-flaco-93/resumen.texto: Consul in 93 BC and governor of Citerior for a decade. His name appears on the second Botorrita bronze (87 BC) as the magistrate who set the formula by which the senate of Contrebia judged a water dispute between neighbouring communities. According to Appian (Iberica 100), a Flaccus, identified with him, killed twenty thousand rebel Celtiberians and punished the people of Belgida, who had burned their senators alive for hesitating to join the revolt.

personas/quinto-sertorio/resumen.texto: Roman general of Marius’s faction who from 80 BC made Hispania the base of his war against Sulla’s regime, with a senate of his own and the support of Lusitanians and Celtiberians. According to Plutarch (Sertorius 11–14), he won over the Hispanics with a white hind that he said had been sent by Diana, opened a school in Osca for the sons of the nobles, who were at the same time hostages, and had a bodyguard consecrated to him according to the Iberian custom of devotio. He defeated Metellus Pius and Pompey several times; Perperna murdered him at a banquet in 72 BC. His image as an enlightened rebel comes from Plutarch and from the fragments of Sallust; historians debate whether he sought a Hispanic state or only a base from which to return to Rome.

personas/quinto-cecilio-metelo-pio/resum.texto: Proconsul of Ulterior who from 79 BC fought Sertorius, at first with little success and then, together with Pompey, until Sertorius’s death. He is credited with the founding of Metellinum (Medellín).

personas/pompeyo-magno/resumen.texto: Roman general sent against Sertorius in 77 BC. He suffered setbacks at Lauro and Sucro, then took the Celtiberian cities allied with Sertorius (Uxama, Clunia, Termes, Calagurris) and in 72 BC defeated Perperna. He raised a trophy at the pass of the Pyrenees and founded Pompaelo (Pamplona); years later he was Caesar’s rival in the civil war.

personas/marco-perperna/resumen.texto: Lieutenant of Sertorius, who killed him at a banquet in Osca in 72 BC to take command. Pompey defeated him soon afterwards and had him executed, and burned unread the letters that Perperna had offered him from Sertorius to Roman senators (Plutarch, Pompey 20).

personas/publio-carisio/resumen.texto: Legate of Augustus in the wars against the Asturians, who took Lancia in 25 BC (Florus, Orosius) and founded Emerita Augusta for veterans. According to Cassius Dio (LIV.5), his harshness provoked the Asturian rebellion of 22 BC.

personas/marco-vipsanio-agripa/resumen.texto: Augustus’s right-hand man, who in 19 BC ended the Cantabrian wars. According to Cassius Dio (LIV.11), he first had to overcome the resistance of his own soldiers, decimated a legion, killed almost all the Cantabrians of fighting age and brought the rest down to the plain; he refused a triumph.

personas/eduardo-saavedra/resumen.texto: Spanish civil engineer who studied the Roman road from Uxama to Augustobriga and who, in 1861–1867, commissioned by the Royal Academy of History, excavated the hill of Garray. His excavations confirmed that Numantia was there, as authors had argued since the 16th century against an old tradition that placed it in Zamora. He was also an Arabist and historian, and in 1906 he presided over the official commission that re-excavated the city.

personas/adolf-schulten/resumen.texto: German historian who excavated in 1905–1912 the Roman camps around Numantia and published them in four volumes, besides searching unsuccessfully for Tartessos in Doñana and launching the Fontes Hispaniae Antiquae. He dominated Spanish ancient history for decades, and Franco’s regime awarded him a decoration in 1940. Today he is credited with documenting the camps and compiling the sources, and he is criticized for his forced readings of the texts, his identification of Tartessos with Atlantis, his racial ideas about Iberians and Celts, and his little interest in the native city.

personas/blas-taracena/resumen.texto: Archaeologist from Soria who excavated at Numantia with the official commission, studied Numantine pottery and defined the culture of the castros of Soria. His Carta arqueológica de España: Soria (1941) is the basis for the study of the Arevaci and Pelendones; he later directed the Museo Arqueológico Nacional.

personas/pere-bosch-gimpera/resumen.texto: Catalan prehistorian who proposed the first synthesis of the pre-Roman peoples of the peninsula, with successive Celtic waves coming from central Europe. He collaborated with Schulten on the Fontes Hispaniae Antiquae and was rector of the University of Barcelona; he went into exile in 1939 and lived in Mexico from 1941. His scheme of invasions was abandoned by later archaeology.

personas/antonio-tovar/resumen.texto: Spanish linguist who studied the pre-Roman languages of the peninsula and continued the ancient geography of Hispania that Schulten had left. He argued that Lusitanian was a non-Celtic Indo-European language, because it preserves initial p; he was rector of Salamanca under Francoism and later distanced himself from the regime.

personas/francisco-villar/resumen.texto: Spanish linguist, professor at Salamanca, specialist in the Indo-European languages of the peninsula. He holds that Lusitanian is not Celtic (with Rosa Pedrero he linked it to Ligurian) and that river names reveal an Indo-European layer older than the Celtic one, extending even into lands that were later Iberian. That ancient layer is disputed by those who see in these names a Celtic or pre-Indo-European origin.

personas/martin-almagro-gorbea/resumen.texto: Spanish archaeologist, co-editor with Gonzalo Ruiz Zapatero of The Celts: Hispania and Europe (1993). He proposed that the Celtic element in the peninsula formed by accumulation, over a “proto-Celtic” substratum of the Bronze Age, rather than through an invasion. It is objected that this “proto-Celtic” has no direct linguistic proof and that it stretches the term Celtic.

personas/francisco-burillo/resumen.texto: Aragonese archaeologist who has directed the excavations at Segeda since the late 1990s and wrote Los celtíberos: etnias y estados (1998). He argues that the Celtiberian cities were city-states and that the synoecism of Segeda was the real cause of the war of 153 BC. He also promoted the study of the now depopulated Serranía Celtibérica.

personas/alberto-lorrio/resumen.texto: Spanish archaeologist, author of Los celtíberos (1997), the reference archaeological synthesis of that people. He distinguishes phases of Celtiberian culture from the 7th century BC onwards, based on necropolises, weapons and settlements.

personas/francisco-calo-lourido/resumen.texto: Galician archaeologist and anthropologist who excavated castros such as Baroña and studied castro culture. In “Os celtas. Unha (re)visión dende Galicia” (2010) he reviewed the question of the Celts in Galicia from the archaeology of the castros.

personas/jorge-de-alarcao/resumen.texto: Portuguese archaeologist at the University of Coimbra, author of Roman Portugal (1988) and of studies on the geography of the pre-Roman peoples of the west and their organization into populi and castella.

personas/miguel-de-cervantes/resumen.texto: Spanish writer, author of Don Quixote. Around 1582 he wrote The Siege of Numantia, a tragedy about the fall of the city that turned the Numantines into a symbol of Hispanic resistance.

hechos/celtas-de-iberia-en-las-fuentes/t.texto: The Celts of the peninsula according to the ancient authors

hechos/celtas-de-iberia-en-las-fuentes/r.texto: Herodotus (II.33 and IV.49) places the Celts “beyond the Pillars of Heracles”, neighbours of the Cynetes, the westernmost peoples of Europe. Strabo (Book III) calls Celtic the peoples of the southwest and the northwest and describes the Celtiberians; Pliny (III.13) says that the Celtici of Baeturia came from the Celtiberians of Lusitania, “as their rites, their language and the names of their cities prove”; Mela (III) places Celtici on the Galician coast, and Diodorus (V.33, from Posidonius), Appian (Iberica 2) and Lucan (IV.9–10) explain the name of the Celtiberians as a mixture of Celts and Iberians. Martial calls himself “born of Celts and Iberians” (IV.55). For the Greeks “Celt” was a broad label for the barbarians of the west, and none of these authors defined it by language, as modern linguistics does; that is why the “Celts” of the sources do not always coincide with those of the linguists.

hechos/celtizacion-de-la-peninsula/titul.texto: How the Celtic languages reached the peninsula: the debate

hechos/celtizacion-de-la-peninsula/resum.texto: What is certain is that in the 2nd century BC a Celtic language, Celtiberian, was spoken on the eastern Meseta; that the western half of the peninsula is full of Celtic names (those ending in -briga, “fortified height”); and that the east and the south spoke Iberian and other non-Indo-European languages. How and when they arrived is debated: Bosch Gimpera (Etnología de la península ibérica, 1932) saw waves of invaders with the urnfields; Almagro-Gorbea and Ruiz Zapatero (1993) prefer a gradual Celticization over local substrates; Cunliffe and Koch (Celtic from the West, 2010) propose that Celtic arose on the Atlantic seaboard, and Koch reads Tartessian as Celtic, a reading rejected by Untermann, de Hoz, Eska and Correa; Villar (2000) defends an earlier non-Celtic Indo-European layer. Genetics (Olalde et al., 2019) shows the great arrival of steppe ancestry around 2500–2000 BC and a smaller contribution from central Europe at the end of the Bronze Age or the beginning of the Iron Age, which the authors relate to the urnfields, but it cannot say what language anyone spoke.

hechos/lengua-celtibera/titulo.texto: Celtiberian, the written Celtic language of the peninsula

hechos/lengua-celtibera/resumen.texto: Celtiberian is the only ancient Celtic language of the peninsula with texts of some length: the Botorrita bronzes, the Luzaga bronze, the tesserae, the coin legends and the rock inscriptions of Peñalba de Villastar. It is an “archaic” Celtic language that preserves the Indo-European kw (like Irish and unlike Gaulish), which was used to classify it among the “Q” Celtic languages. Of Gallaecian, the language of the northwest, only names of people, places and gods survive.

hechos/celtiberos/resumen.texto: Celtic-speaking peoples of the eastern Meseta and the Iberian System (Arevaci, Belli, Titii, Lusones and, according to some, Pelendones), whose archaeological culture takes shape from the 7th century BC in the upper Jalón and upper Tajo. They lived in castros and later in fortified cities with a senate and magistrates, buried their warriors with their weapons, and wrote their language from the 2nd century BC. Diodorus (V.33–34) describes them as the best horsemen and infantry, hospitable to strangers and cruel to enemies, with swords of tempered iron; his literary image comes from Posidonius and mixes observation with commonplaces about barbarians. The ancients explained their name as a mixture of Celts and Iberians, but it is a name given by Greeks and Romans, it does not appear in their inscriptions, and their language is Celtic (they took the script from the Iberians); that is why most modern authors read it as “the Celts of Iberia” and not as a mixed people.

hechos/arevacos/resumen.texto: The most powerful Celtiberian people according to Strabo (III.4.13), in the upper Duero, with cities such as Numantia, Termes, Uxama and Clunia. They led the resistance to Rome between 153 and 133 BC and rose again with Sertorius; Pliny (III.27) says that they took their name from the river Areva.

hechos/belos-y-titos/resumen.texto: Two Celtiberian peoples of the Jalón and Huerva valleys. The Belli had their main city at Segeda, whose attempt to absorb the Titii and fortify itself provoked the war of 153 BC; both signed the peace of Marcellus in 151 BC, and afterwards they disappear as peoples in the sources. For many authors Contrebia Belaisca was a city of the Belli.

hechos/lusones/resumen.texto: Celtiberian people whom Strabo places at the sources of the Tagus and Appian on the Ebro; their exact territory is debated. They were among the first Celtiberians to clash with Rome, in the war of 181–179 BC.

hechos/pelendones/resumen.texto: People of the north of present-day Soria, at the headwaters of the Duero, whom archaeology associates with the castros of Soria. Pliny (III.26) counts Numantia among the Pelendones and Ptolemy among the Arevaci, a contradiction explained by changing frontiers or by an error in one of the sources.

hechos/vacceos/resumen.texto: People of the middle Duero valley, with large cities such as Pintia, Cauca, Intercatia and Palantia. Diodorus (V.34) says that each year they shared out the land, pooled the harvest and punished with death anyone who hid something; the passage is debated (perhaps an idealization by Posidonius), and Joaquín Costa read it as a precedent for agrarian collectivism. Aelian (On the Nature of Animals X.22) says they exposed their fallen in battle to vultures, as Silius Italicus says of the Celtiberians, a rite that appears on stelae and vessels from the region.

hechos/vetones/resumen.texto: People of the western Meseta (Ávila, Salamanca, Cáceres), with large castros such as Las Cogotas, Ulaca, La Mesa de Miranda and El Raso. They are known for the verracos, some four hundred granite sculptures of bulls and pigs whose function is debated: for some, markers of pasture land and protection of livestock; for others, funerary monuments, in Roman times. The sources name them among the allies of the Lusitanians and the Celtiberians.

hechos/carpetanos/resumen.texto: People of the centre of the Meseta, around Toletum (Toledo), Complutum and the middle Tagus basin. Hannibal defeated them at the battle of the Tagus (220 BC), and Rome subjugated them in the campaigns of 193–179 BC. Their language is known only from names, which have an Indo-European appearance and are partly Celtic.

hechos/lusitanos/resumen.texto: People of the west of the peninsula between the Duero and the Tagus, who resisted Rome from 155 BC until Viriathus, and who gave their name to the province of Lusitania. Strabo (III.3.6) describes them sacrificing prisoners and divining by their entrails, with small shields and helmets of sinew, and attributes to all the northern mountaineers (III.3.7) acorn bread and beer; their language is known from a few inscriptions in Latin letters. Whether Lusitanian is Celtic is debated: it preserves the Indo-European p, which Celtic lost, so Tovar, Gorrochategui, Villar and Blanca María Prósper (1999) see it as a non-Celtic Indo-European language (Villar and Rosa Pedrero, 2001, link it to Ligurian); Untermann (1987) stressed the place and personal names it shares with Celtic, and Dagmar Wodtko (in Celtic from the West, 2010) holds that almost no Lusitanian names are non-Celtic, while Krzysztof Witczak (1999) replied that those coincidences in names do not prove kinship.

hechos/galaicos/resumen.texto: Peoples of the northwest of the peninsula, north of the Duero, whom Rome came to know through Brutus’s expedition in 137 BC and who lived in castros. Mela and Pliny call several of them Celtic (the Supertamarici and Nerii Celtici, the Artabri), and many of their ancient toponyms have Celtic roots; other names keep the p and seem Lusitanian. Whether they were “Celts” is debated: nineteenth-century Galician Celticism (Manuel Murguía, Historia de Galicia, from 1865) made them ancestors of a Celtic Galicia distinct from the rest of Spain, and since the 1980s, according to Francisco Calo Lourido (Os celtas. Unha (re)visión dende Galicia, 2010), Galician archaeology has split between those who stress the local continuity of castro culture and relativize the label, and those who give weight to names, gods and what the ancient authors say.

hechos/astures/resumen.texto: Peoples of the northwest (Asturias, León, Zamora and Trás-os-Montes), organized into gentes and gentilitates, whom Rome conquered in the wars of 29–19 BC. Their names and gods are Indo-European and largely Celtic. Pliny (III.28) counts twenty-two peoples and two hundred and forty thousand free persons in their judicial district (conventus).

hechos/cantabros/resumen.texto: A people of the Cantabrian mountains, the last in the peninsula to be subdued (29-19 BC). Strabo (III.4.17-18) describes them with traits that modern scholars have read as matriarchal: the women worked the land, husbands gave a dowry to their wives, daughters inherited, and sisters arranged marriages for their brothers. He also says that mothers killed their children before they could be captured, and that the crucified sang hymns. Their language is known only from names, which look Indo-European; whether they were Celts, and how much Strabo's stereotype of the savage mountaineer weighs, is debated.

hechos/celticos-del-suroeste/resumen.texto: Peoples of Baeturia, between the Guadiana and the Guadalquivir, and of the Alentejo. Pliny (III.13) derives them from the Celtiberians on the basis of their rites, their language and their town names (Nertobriga, Segida, Seria). The archaeology of their fortified hillforts (such as Castrejón de Capote) shows contacts with the Meseta from the 4th century BC, although it is unclear whether there was a migration or a diffusion.

hechos/iberos/resumen.texto: Peoples of the east and south of the peninsula, from Languedoc to Andalusia (Indicetes, Ilergetes, Edetani, Contestani, Bastetani, Oretani and others), who spoke a non-Indo-European language, Iberian, still untranslated. They wrote from the 5th century BC onward in their own semi-syllabaries and in an alphabet taken from the Greeks, lived in towns and oppida, and left a sculpture of their own (the Lady of Elche, the Lady of Baza, the votive offerings of Cerro de los Santos) and the falcata. They were not Celts, but they were their neighbours: the Celtiberians took writing from them and, according to the ancients, part of their name.

hechos/turdetanos/resumen.texto: A people of the Guadalquivir valley, heirs of Tartessus, whom Strabo (III.1.6) considers the most cultured in the peninsula, with laws in verse and writings said to be six thousand years old. Rome romanized them early. Cato fought the Celtiberians who were hired as mercenaries by them in 195 BC.

hechos/cultura-castrena/resumen.texto: A culture of the northwest of the peninsula (Galicia, northern Portugal, western Asturias) from the end of the Bronze Age to the Roman period, with fortified settlements on heights (castros) of round stone houses. Around the 2nd century BC large settlements (citânias, oppida) such as Briteiros and Sanfins grew. From the last centuries before Rome and the early Roman period come their gold torcs, their statues of warriors and their monumental saunas. Whether it was “Celtic” depends on what one means by the term: its language had much that was Celtic, but its architecture and material culture are local and Atlantic.

hechos/adopcion-de-la-escritura-celtiber.texto: By the first half of the 2nd century BC the Celtiberians had adapted the northeastern Iberian semi-syllabary to their language, in an eastern and a western variant. They used it on coins, tesserae, bronzes and graffiti until the 1st century BC, when they switched to the Latin alphabet. It is one of the few cases in which an ancient Celtic people left written texts of its own.

hechos/armas-de-los-pueblos-hispanos/tit.texto: The caetra, the falcata and the soliferreum

hechos/armas-de-los-pueblos-hispanos/res.texto: Ancient authors describe the Hispanic warriors with the caetra, a small round shield (Strabo III.3.6); swords of iron so well tempered that they cut through helmets and shields, which, according to Diodorus (V.33), were buried so that rust would take away the weak parts; and the soliferreum, a javelin made of a single piece of iron. The falcata, a curved single-edged sword, was above all Iberian; the name is modern, from the 19th century. The archaeology of the Celtiberian and Iberian necropolises confirms this armament and its variety according to period and region.

hechos/adopcion-del-gladius-hispaniensis.texto: Polybius (VI.23) calls the short sword with a point and two edges used by the legionaries “Iberian”, and a fragment of his preserved in the Suda says that the Romans took it from the Hispanians in the time of the war against Hannibal. Livy (XXXI.34) recounts the terror of the Macedonians before the wounds of that “Spanish sword” in 200 BC. Archaeology relates it to Celtiberian swords of La Tène type, although the exact moment of adoption is debated.

hechos/devotio-iberica/titulo.texto: The devotio: to die with the chief

hechos/devotio-iberica/resumen.texto: A custom by which a group of warriors dedicated their lives to a chief and were not to survive him. Valerius Maximus (II.6.11) says that the Celtiberians regarded it as sacrilege to survive the chief for whom they had dedicated their lives, and Plutarch (Sertorius 14) says that Sertorius had thousands of such guards. Strabo (III.4.18) attributes the custom to the Iberians in general. Modern scholars call it the Iberian devotio and compare it with the soldurii of Caesar's Aquitanians, and with the fides, the personal loyalty that Roman sources attribute to the Celtiberians.

hechos/exposicion-a-los-buitres/titulo.texto: The fallen in battle, left to the vultures

hechos/exposicion-a-los-buitres/resumen.texto: Silius Italicus (Punica III.340-343) and Aelian say that the Celtiberians and the Vaccaei did not cremate their dead who fell in battle but left them to the vultures, which carried their souls to heaven, while they cremated the rest. Scenes of vultures over fallen warriors appear on painted vases from Numantia and on stelae from the region, which suggests that the texts record a real rite.

hechos/campana-de-amilcar-en-iberia/titu.texto: Hamilcar Barca in the peninsula: Istolatius and Indortes

hechos/campana-de-amilcar-en-iberia/resu.texto: Hamilcar landed at Gadir in 237 BC and, in almost nine years, according to Polybius (II.1), subdued much of the south and the east. Diodorus (XXV.10) says that he first defeated the Celt Istolatius and his brother, who commanded Iberians and Tartessians, and then Indortes, whom he had blinded and crucified. Polybius (II.1) summarizes the campaign. He died in 229 BC fighting the Oretani.

hechos/batalla-del-tajo/resumen.texto: Hannibal, returning from a campaign against the Vaccaei in which he took Helmantica (Salamanca) and Arbucala, was attacked as he crossed the Tagus by a coalition of Carpetani, Vaccaei and Olcades. According to Polybius (III.14), who gives a figure of one hundred thousand enemies, he defeated them by letting them cross the river and attacking them in the water with his cavalry and his elephants.

hechos/sitio-de-sagunto/resumen.texto: Hannibal besieged Arse (Saguntum), an Iberian town allied with Rome, for eight months and took it in 219 BC. It was the trigger of the Second Punic War, which brought the Romans to the peninsula in 218 BC. Livy (XXI.14) says that its inhabitants burned their possessions and threw themselves into the fire, a heroic account that anticipates that of Numantia.

hechos/mercenarios-celtiberos-de-los-esc.texto: The Celtiberians, Rome's first mercenaries, and the fall of the Scipios

According to Livy (XXIV.49), in 213 BC the Roman generals in Hispania, the brothers Publius and Gnaeus Scipio, attracted young Celtiberians with the same pay that Carthage gave them, and they were the first mercenaries Rome had in its camps. In 211 BC, when Gnaeus was leading them against Hasdrubal, Hasdrubal paid their chiefs to send them home, and the departure of some twenty thousand Celtiberians left the two brothers without forces: both died in the defeats of the upper Baetis (Livy XXV.32-36). Livy attributes the disaster to the “perfidy” of the barbarians, a judgment of the Roman tradition which also used this explanation for a Roman defeat.

hechos/revuelta-de-indibil-y-mandonio/ti.texto: The revolt of Indibilis and Mandonius

hechos/revuelta-de-indibil-y-mandonio/re.texto: The Ilergete chiefs, allies of Scipio against Carthage, rebelled when the Romans stayed in the peninsula after the Carthaginians were expelled. Defeated in 206 BC and pardoned, they rose again in 205 BC: Indibilis died in battle and Mandonius was handed over and executed (Livy XXVIII-XXIX). It was the first major indigenous revolt against Rome in Hispania.

hechos/campana-de-caton-en-hispania/resu.texto: The consul Cato landed at Emporion, defeated the rebels of Hispania Citerior and, according to Livy (XXXIV.17), had the walls of the cities north of the Ebro torn down in a single day. In the south he offered the Celtiberian mercenaries of the Turdetani double pay to change sides, and then marched on to Segontia, in Celtiberia. His boast that he had taken more towns than the days he had spent in Hispania (Plutarch, Cato 10) is his own propaganda.

hechos/guerras-celtiberas/resumen.texto: A series of wars between Rome and the Celtiberian peoples of the eastern Meseta: the first (181-179 BC), which ended with the treaties of Gracchus; the second (154-151 BC), begun over the wall of Segeda; and the Numantine War (143-133 BC), which ended with the destruction of Numantia. Polybius, who was in Numantia, called the war of 153-151 BC the “war of fire” because of its severity (XXXV.1). We know them above all from Appian and from the summaries of Livy.

hechos/primera-guerra-celtibera/resumen.texto: The Lusones and other Celtiberians clashed with the praetors of Hispania Citerior. Quintus Fulvius Flaccus defeated them in 181 BC, and Tiberius Sempronius Gracchus subdued the rest in 180-179 BC (Livy XL). Polybius, cited by Strabo (III.4.13), said that Gracchus had destroyed three hundred towns, and Posidonius already mocked the figure: they counted as towns what were really towers.

hechos/tratados-de-graco/resumen.texto: Tiberius Gracchus ended the First Celtiberian War with agreements with each people: tribute, auxiliary troops, and a ban on founding new towns (Appian, Iberica 43-44). He distributed land to the poor and founded Gracurris. That peace lasted until 154 BC, and in the wars that followed the Celtiberians asked to return to it.

hechos/rebelion-de-olindico/resumen.texto: The Celtiberian Olindicus stirred up his people with a silver spear which, he said, had come to him from the sky. He died after entering the Roman camp at night to kill the general. Florus (I.33.13) and the summary of Livy's book XLIII are the only sources.

hechos/segunda-guerra-celtibera/resumen.texto: A war between Rome and the Belli, Titti and Arevaci that began when Segeda extended its wall. After the defeat of Nobilior by Caro (153 BC) and his failure before Numantia, the consul Marcellus negotiated a peace with the three peoples in 151 BC. His successor Lucullus attacked the Vaccaei without orders from the Senate. Polybius (XXXV.1) called it the “war of fire” and says that in Rome nobody wanted to enlist for service in Hispania.

hechos/sinecismo-de-segeda/titulo.texto: The wall and the synoecism of Segeda

hechos/sinecismo-de-segeda/resumen.texto: Segeda, a town of the Belli, gathered the neighbouring peoples within its precinct, among them the Titti, and began a wall forty stadia long, some seven kilometres (Appian, Iberica 44). The Senate forbade it and demanded the tribute and troops of the treaty of Gracchus. The Segedans replied that the treaty forbade founding towns, not fortifying existing ones. The archaeology of Burillo found the new town beside the old one, at Belmonte de Gracián and Mara.

hechos/batalla-de-segeda/resumen.texto: On 23 August 153 BC, the day of the festival of Vulcan, the Segedan chief Caro, at the head of about twenty thousand infantry and five thousand horsemen, ambushed in a forest the army of almost thirty thousand men of the consul Nobilior, and killed, according to Appian (Iberica 45), six thousand Roman citizens. Caro died in the pursuit, when the cavalry guarding the baggage fell upon his men. From then on Roman generals avoided fighting on that day.

hechos/cambio-del-comienzo-del-ano-consu.texto: The consuls take office on 1 January

Because of the urgency of the war in Hispania, in 153 BC the consuls began to take office on 1 January instead of 15 March, so that Nobilior could reach Segeda sooner (summary of Livy's book XLVII). From then on the Roman year, and the calendar that the West inherited, begins in January.

hechos/paz-de-marcelo/resumen.texto: The consul Marcus Claudius Marcellus, after taking Ocilis and pressing Numantia, accepted the surrender of the Arevaci, Belli and Titti on moderate terms, with a payment that Posidonius, cited by Strabo (III.4.13), puts at six hundred talents. The peace lasted eight years. Appian (Iberica 50) says that Marcellus wanted to end the war before his successor arrived.

hechos/masacre-de-cauca/resumen.texto: The consul Lucullus, without an order from the Senate and in search of booty, attacked the Vaccaei of Cauca, who were not at war with Rome. He accepted their surrender, hostages and one hundred talents of silver, let his soldiers in, and killed the men of the town: of twenty thousand, says Appian (Iberica 52), few escaped. The other Vaccaean towns no longer surrendered; at Intercatia the young Scipio Aemilianus defeated a Vaccaean warrior in single combat.

hechos/guerra-lusitana/resumen.texto: A war between Rome and the Lusitanians that began with the raids of Punicus and Caesarus in Hispania Ulterior (155-153 BC), continued with the massacre of Galba (150 BC), and had its main phase under Viriathus (147-139 BC), who defeated several praetors and consuls. It ended with his murder and the surrender of Tautalus. We know it from Appian, from Diodorus (who drew on Posidonius) and from the summaries of Livy. Latin authors present it as a war against “bandits”.

hechos/masacre-de-galba/resumen.texto: The praetor Servius Sulpicius Galba promised land to the Lusitanians who asked for peace, divided them into three groups, had them lay down their arms and ordered them killed. Few escaped, among them Viriathus (Appian, Iberica 59-60). The sources do not agree on the number of dead. Galba was prosecuted in Rome in 149 BC, with Cato among the accusers, and acquitted. That same year the Calpurnian law created the first permanent court against the abuses of governors. The sources do not say that it was because of Galba, although many historians connect the two.

hechos/batalla-de-tribola/resumen.texto: Viriathus, newly elected chief, lured the praetor Gaius Vetilius into an ambush in a gorge near Tribola, in Hispania Ulterior, and killed him with a large part of his army (Appian, Iberica 63). It was the first of a series of victories that made him feared in Rome.

hechos/paz-de-viriato/resumen.texto: Besieged at Erisana, the proconsul Fabius Maximus Servilianus signed a peace with Viriathus that recognized him as a friend of the Roman people and left the Lusitanians the lands they occupied. The Roman people ratified it (Appian, Iberica 69). The following year the Senate authorized Servilius Caepio to break it.

hechos/asesinato-de-viriato/resumen.texto: Audax, Ditalco and Minurus, sent by Viriathus to negotiate with Servilius Caepio, accepted his bribe and killed him while he slept. According to Appian (Iberica 74-75), the Lusitanians burned him on a great pyre with sacrifices and held single combats beside his tomb; Diodorus (XXXIII.21a) speaks of two hundred pairs of combatants. The phrase “Rome does not pay traitors” is a modern version; Eutropius says that the murderers were told that Rome had never liked a general to be killed by his own men.

hechos/guerra-numantina/resumen.texto: The last Celtiberian war, in which Numantia and Termes resisted for ten years a succession of Roman generals. Metellus subdued the Arevaci except those two towns (143-142 BC); Quintus Pompeius agreed a peace in secret and then denied it (140 BC); and Mancinus surrendered his whole army (137 BC). Rome ended it in 133 BC with Scipio Aemilianus and the siege of the city. Florus (I.34.2) says that Numantia, with four thousand Celtiberians, alone resisted for eleven years an army of forty thousand; the figures of Florus and Orosius inflate both the Numantines and their conquerors.

hechos/rendicion-de-mancino/resumen.texto: The consul Mancinus, surrounded by the Numantines, saved about twenty thousand soldiers with a treaty negotiated by his quaestor Tiberius Gracchus, whom the Numantines trusted for the memory of his father. The Senate annulled it and handed Mancinus over, naked and bound, before the gates of Numantia, which did not receive him (Appian, Iberica 80-83; Plutarch, Tiberius Gracchus 5-7). The episode lies at the origin of Tiberius Gracchus' political career.

hechos/expedicion-de-bruto-al-noroeste/r.texto: The consul Decimus Junius Brutus led the first Roman campaign north of the Douro. His soldiers feared to cross the Limia, which they believed was the Lethe, the river of forgetfulness, until he snatched the standard from a standard-bearer and carried it to the other side (Livy, summary of book LV; Florus I.33.12). Appian (Iberica 72) says that the women of the Bracari fought alongside the men and preferred to kill themselves rather than be captured.

hechos/sitio-de-numancia/resumen.texto: Scipio Aemilianus arrived in 134 BC, disciplined a demoralized army, razed the fields of the Vaccaei and surrounded Numantia with a wall nine kilometres long, seven camps and barriers over the Douro. According to Appian (Iberica 90-98), the Numantines, who at the start of the war numbered no more than eight thousand men against sixty thousand, ate leather and then corpses, surrendered in the summer of 133 BC and many killed themselves. Scipio kept fifty for his triumph, sold the rest and razed the city. Florus (I.34) and Orosius (V.7) say instead that nobody surrendered and that all died by setting the city on fire, the version Cervantes adopted; historians prefer Appian's, which derives from Polybius, an eyewitness to the events. The camps excavated by Schulten confirm the siege.

hechos/castigo-de-lutia/resumen.texto: When Retogenes managed to break out of the siege and asked the Arevacian towns for help, only the young men of Lutia wanted to go. Warned by the elders of the town, Scipio arrived with troops, demanded that four hundred young men be handed over, and had their hands cut off (Appian, Iberica 94). Lutia has not been securely located.

hechos/campanas-de-tito-didio/resumen.texto: The proconsul Titus Didius defeated the Arevaci, of whom he killed about twenty thousand according to Appian (Iberica 99-100). He forced Termes to come down to the plain, sold the inhabitants of Colenda into slavery after a nine-month siege, and massacred those of a neighbouring town, whom he had lured with the promise of land. He celebrated his triumph in 93 BC.

hechos/pleito-de-las-aguas-de-contrebia/.texto: The water dispute before the senate of Contrebia

In May 87 BC the senate of Contrebia Belaisca, acting as a jury at the request of the governor Gaius Valerius Flaccus, ruled in favour of the Salluienses in their dispute with the Allavonenses over land bought from the Sosinestani to dig a canal. It is the first documented trial in Roman Hispania and shows Celtiberian judges applying a formula of Roman law.

hechos/guerra-sertoriana/resumen.texto: Quintus Sertorius, a general of Marius' side proscribed by Sulla, established himself in Hispania with the support of Lusitanians and Celtiberians, and for years defeated Metellus Pius and Pompey. Among his allies were the Arevacian towns of Clunia, Uxama and Termes, and the Vasconic Calagurris, and in 77 BC he took Contrebia Leucade. Plutarch and the fragments of Sallust present him as a just leader, beloved by the Hispanians. The war ended with his murder and the defeat of Perperna.

hechos/escuela-de-osca/resumen.texto: According to Plutarch (Sertorius 14), Sertorius gathered the sons of the Hispanic nobles at Osca (Huesca), dressed them in the Roman manner and had them taught Greek and Latin, both to educate them and to keep them as hostages. When his allies began to abandon him, he had some of them killed or sold.

hechos/asesinato-de-sertorio/resumen.texto: His lieutenant Marcus Perperna killed him at a banquet in Osca in 72 BC. According to Plutarch (Sertorius 26-27), Pompey quickly defeated Perperna and burned unread the letters from Sertorius that implicated Roman senators; without their chief, the Hispanic coalition fell apart.

hechos/sitio-de-calagurris/resumen.texto: Calagurris, a Vasconic town allied with Sertorius, resisted the siege by Afranius, legate of Pompey, until after his death. Valerius Maximus (VII.6) and Juvenal (XV) say that its inhabitants ate their dead. Roman authors placed it beside Numantia as an example of resistance to the point of the inhuman.

hechos/campana-de-cesar-en-lusitania/tit.texto: Caesar's campaign in Lusitania and Gallaecia

hechos/campana-de-cesar-en-lusitania/res.texto: As governor of Hispania Ulterior, Julius Caesar attacked the peoples of Mons Herminius (the Serra da Estrela), pursued those who fled across the Douro, and reached Brigantium, in Gallaecia, by sea (Cassius Dio XXXVII.52-53). Suetonius (Caesar 54) says that he sacked Lusitanian towns that were not making war on him, and it is debated whether he was mainly seeking booty to pay his debts.

hechos/guerras-cantabras/resumen.texto: The last war of conquest in the peninsula, against the Cantabri and the Asturians. Augustus directed it in person in 26-25 BC from Segisama, until he fell ill and withdrew to Tarraco. His legates Antistius and Carisius took hillforts and the town of Lancia, and in 25 BC Augustus closed the doors of the temple of Janus. There were revolts in 24, 22 and 19 BC, until Agrippa subdued the last Cantabri. Cassius Dio (LIII-LIV) is the main source; Florus and Orosius follow the lost Livy, and archaeology has found camps and sieges such as that of Monte Bernorio.

hechos/monte-medulio/resumen.texto: Florus (II.33) and Orosius (VI.21) say that the Romans surrounded the last resistance fighters on Mount Medulius with a fifteen-mile ditch, and that these preferred to kill themselves with swords, fire and yew poison rather than surrender. Cassius Dio does not mention it. Modern scholars date it to 25 or 22 BC. The place has not been identified (Las Médulas, the Teleno and other mountains of Galicia, León and Cantabria have been proposed), and the account repeats the literary model of Numantia, so its historicity is debated.

hechos/fundacion-de-emerita-augusta/resu.texto: In 25 BC Augustus settled the veterans discharged from the Cantabrian wars in a colony on the Guadiana, Emerita Augusta, which became the capital of the new province of Lusitania (Cassius Dio LIII.26).

hechos/fin-de-las-guerras-cantabras/resu.texto: The Cantabri who had been sold into slavery killed their masters and returned to the war. According to Cassius Dio (LIV.11), Agrippa first had to overcome the discouragement of his own soldiers, decimated a legion, killed almost all the men of fighting age and forced the rest to come down from the mountains; he declined a triumph. With this the conquest of the peninsula ended, two centuries after Rome's arrival.

hechos/poblacion-del-noroeste-segun-plin.texto: The free population of the northwest according to Pliny

Pliny (III.28), who had been procurator in Hispania Tarraconensis, gives the only ancient population figure for a region of the peninsula: two hundred and forty thousand free people in the conventus of the Astures, one hundred and sixty-six thousand in the Lucensis and two hundred and eighty-five thousand in the Bracarensis, some seven hundred thousand in total. They probably come from a Roman census, Augustan or Flavian, and do not count slaves. They are among the few ancient figures that many historians consider plausible, unlike the figures for armies and war dead, which are inflated or rounded.

hechos/cifras-de-numancia/resumen.texto: Appian (Iberica 97) says that Numantia had no more than eight thousand fighting men at the start of the war, against sixty thousand men of Scipio's, with his allies. Florus (I.34.2) speaks of four thousand Numantines against forty thousand Romans, the same figures that the summary of Livy's book LV gives for the defeat of Mancinus, and Appian says that Caro gathered twenty thousand infantry and five thousand horsemen in 153 BC. The excavated city covers some six to eight hectares, and it is estimated that a couple of thousand people lived there. David Henige (1998), studying Caesar's figures, showed how the round numbers of ancient authors about barbarians serve to magnify either the victor or the vanquished, and the figures for Numantia have the same problem.

hechos/excavaciones-de-numancia/resumen.texto: The engineer Eduardo Saavedra identified and excavated the hill of Garray in 1861-1867. Adolf Schulten, with the support of the Kaiser, excavated the Roman siege camps and those of Renieblas in 1905-1912, while an official Spanish commission, presided over by Saavedra, with José Ramón Mélida among its archaeologists, had been excavating the city since 1906, partly as a nationalist reaction to the foreign archaeologist. By then Numantia, since Cervantes and the historiography of the 19th century, was a Spanish national symbol, a reading that current historiography considers anachronistic. In 1905 Alfonso XIII inaugurated a monument to the heroes of Numantia on the hill.

hechos/hallazgo-de-la-dama-de-elche/titu.texto: Discovery of the Lady of Elche

hechos/hallazgo-de-la-dama-de-elche/resu.texto: On 4 August 1897 an Iberian bust of polychrome limestone, from the 5th-4th centuries BC, appeared at La Alcudia (Elche), with a hollow in the back that may have served as an urn. The Louvre bought it at once; it returned to Spain in 1941 in an exchange with the Vichy government and is now in the National Archaeological Museum. In 1995 John F. Moffitt argued that it was a modern forgery, a thesis that pigment analyses and most specialists reject.

hechos/hallazgo-de-botorrita/resumen.texto: In 1970 the first bronze appeared at the Cabezo de las Minas in Botorrita (Zaragoza), the longest Celtiberian text known until then; in 1979 the second, in Latin; in 1992 the third, with some two hundred and fifty names; and in 1994 a fourth fragment. They transformed the study of Celtiberian, which moved from coin legends to extended texts.

hechos/numancia-de-alberti/resumen.texto: In December 1937, during the Civil War, Rafael Alberti premiered at the Teatro de la Zarzuela in Madrid an adaptation of Cervantes' tragedy in which the Numantines represented the besieged republic and the Romans the rebels and their foreign allies. The rebel side also used the symbol: in 1936 a regiment called Numancia renamed the Toledo village of Azaña as Numancia de la Sagra. The myth served opposing causes.

lugares/numancia/resumen.texto: Celtiberian city on the hill of La Muela, in Garray (Soria), above the Douro, with some six to eight hectares excavated, paved streets and houses of stone and adobe. It resisted Rome between 153 and 133 BC until Scipio Aemilianus forced it to surrender through hunger and razed it; a small Roman town was later built on its ruins. Pliny counts it among the Pelendones and Ptolemy among the Arevaci; the siege camps are preserved around it.

lugares/segeda/resumen.texto: Main town of the Belli, between Mara and Belmonte de Gracián (Zaragoza), which minted coins with the name sekaisa. Its expansion and its new wall of some seven kilometres caused the war of 153 BC. The old and the new town have been excavated since the late 1990s under the direction of Francisco Burillo.

lugares/contrebia-belaisca/resumen.texto: Celtiberian town at the Cabezo de las Minas, in Botorrita (Zaragoza), which minted coins as kontebakom bel. The four Botorrita bronzes were found there, among them the first extended Celtiberian text and the Latin judgment of 87 BC. A large adobe building with columns, perhaps public, was also excavated.

lugares/tiermes/resumen.texto: Arevacian town and later Roman municipium at Montejo de Tiermes (Soria), more than 1,200 metres above sea level, with houses and steps carved into the sandstone rock. It resisted together with Numantia in the war of 143-133 BC; in 98-93 BC Titus Didius forced its inhabitants down to the plain.

lugares/segobriga/resumen.texto: Celtiberian and later Roman town at Saelices (Cuenca), which Pliny (III.25) calls the “capital of Celtiberia”. Under Rome it grew rich from the lapis specularis mines, a transparent gypsum used as glass, and it preserves a theatre, an amphitheatre and a forum.

lugares/clunia/resumen.texto: Arevacian town that was Sertorius' refuge in 75 BC and later a Roman colony and the capital of a judicial district, at Peñalba de Castro (Burgos). In AD 68 Galba, who had risen against Nero, was at Clunia when he learned that Rome recognized him as emperor (Suetonius, Plutarch).

lugares/bilbilis/resumen.texto: Roman municipium on the Bámbola hill, next to Calatayud (Zaragoza), heir to a Celtiberian town that minted coins with the name bilbilis. It was the homeland of the poet Martial, who praises the iron of its river Jalón, in which weapons were tempered.

lugares/uxama/resumen.texto: Arevacian and later Roman town next to El Burgo de Osma (Soria), an ally of Sertorius and taken by Pompey in 72 BC. It minted coins with the legend usamus.

lugares/contrebia-leucade/resumen.texto: Celtiberian town at Aguilar del Río Alhama (La Rioja), with a ditch cut into the rock and well-preserved houses. Sertorius took it in 77 BC after a siege recounted in a fragment of Livy.

lugares/pintia/resumen.texto: Vaccaean town at Padilla de Duero (Peñafiel, Valladolid), with its Las Ruedas necropolis, where the tombs of warriors, women and children show Vaccaean society, and stelae linked to the rite of exposing the dead.

lugares/las-cogotas/resumen.texto: Castro de Cardeñosa (Ávila), excavated by Juan Cabré in 1927-1931, which gives its name to two cultures: Cogotas I, of the Bronze Age, with its characteristic decorated pottery, and Cogotas II, of the Vettonian oppidum of the Iron Age, with its necropolises of warriors.

lugares/ulaca/resumen.texto: Large Vettonian oppidum of some sixty hectares at Solosancho (Ávila), with walls, hundreds of houses, a sacrificial altar carved into the rock and a stone sauna. It was abandoned with the Roman conquest in the 1st century BC.

lugares/mesa-de-miranda/resumen.texto: Vettonian hillfort at Chamartín (Ávila), with three walled enclosures and the necropolis of La Osera, one of the largest on the Meseta, with more than two thousand tombs.

lugares/toros-de-guisando/resumen.texto: Four granite verracos at El Tiemblo (Ávila), carved by the Vettones between the 4th and 2nd centuries BC, with Latin inscriptions added in the Roman period. In 1468 Henry IV of Castile recognized there his sister Isabella, the future Isabella I, as heir.

lugares/monte-bernorio/resumen.texto: Large Cantabrian oppidum of more than one hundred hectares at Villarén de Valdivia (Palencia), which gives its name to a type of Iron Age dagger. Recent excavations found a Roman camp and traces of its siege and destruction in the Cantabrian wars, around 26-25 BC.

lugares/las-medulas/resumen.texto: The largest open-cast gold mine of the Roman Empire, in El Bierzo (León), where mountains were brought down with water carried by canals, the ruina montium that Pliny describes (XXXIII.70-78). It is debated whether the labour was mainly forced, from the conquered Astures, or paid. It has been a World Heritage Site since 1997.

lugares/citania-de-briteiros/resumen.texto: Large castro settlement at Guimarães (Portugal), with more than one hundred and fifty round houses, streets, walls and a sauna with the pedra formosa, a decorated slab. Francisco Martins Sarmento excavated it from 1875, at the beginnings of Portuguese archaeology.

lugares/citania-de-sanfins/resumen.texto: Castro settlement at Paços de Ferreira (Portugal), with quarters of houses grouped around family courtyards, walls and a sauna, occupied mainly between the 2nd century BC and the 1st century AD.

lugares/castro-de-santa-tegra/resumen.texto: Gallaecian castro on the Santa Tegra hill, at A Guarda (Pontevedra), above the mouth of the Minho, with hundreds of round houses, some of them reconstructed. Its peak is in the 1st century BC and the 1st century AD, already under Roman influence.

lugares/castro-de-barona/resumen.texto: Gallaecian castro on a small peninsula at Porto do Son (A Coruña), with two walls and about twenty round houses, occupied between the 1st century BC and the 1st century AD.

lugares/castro-de-san-cibrao-de-las/nomb.texto: Castro de San Cibrao de Las

lugares/castro-de-san-cibrao-de-las/resu.texto: One of the largest castros in Galicia, at San Amaro and Punxín (Ourense), with two walled enclosures and quarters of houses. It is sometimes identified with Ptolemy's Lansbrica.

lugares/castro-de-coana/resumen.texto: Castro de Coaña (Asturias), the first one excavated in Asturias, with dozens of round houses. It was declared a monument in 1931.

lugares/chao-samartin/resumen.texto: Castro at Grandas de Salime (Asturias), founded at the end of the Bronze Age and inhabited until the late 2nd century AD, when an earthquake destroyed it. Under Rome it had a house of Roman type, and it is linked to the control of the area's gold mining.

lugares/santuario-de-cabeco-das-fraguas/.texto: Summit of a sierra near Guarda (Portugal) with a Lusitanian cult enclosure and the rock on which the Lusitanian inscription was carved, listing animal offerings to its gods. About twenty altars were found in the area.

lugares/cerro-de-los-santos/resumen.texto: Iberian sanctuary at Montealegre del Castillo (Albacete), from which hundreds of stone votive offerings came, among them the Great Offering Lady. In the 19th century forgeries by a watchmaker from Yecla were mixed in with its authentic pieces, which for decades damaged the reputation of Iberian art.

lugares/sagunto/resumen.texto: Iberian city of the Edetani, allied with Rome, whose siege by Hannibal in 219 BC triggered the Second Punic War. Its coins bear the Iberian name arse and the Latin Saguntum.
